meaning: When a mistake is made or trouble occurs, one must immediately take steps to correct it or clean up the mess.
literal: If one steps on feces, one wipes it off.
usage: This is used to encourage someone to fix a mistake immediately rather than dwelling on it.
igbo: A baa nshị a rịhị

meaning: Delaying or hesitating to execute a plan against someone only gives them more time to survive and thrive.
literal: While one seeks to kill the young he-goat and hides the knife, the life of the young he-goat grows longer.
usage: This is used to advise someone to act swiftly before their target escapes or grows stronger.
igbo: A chọwa igbu nwa mkpi na-ezo mma, ndụ nwa mkpi ana-eto ogologo

meaning: In trying to be overly clever or talkative, one often ends up revealing secrets or saying things best left unsaid.
literal: When one seeks the beauty of speech, one speaks of what was eaten at night.
usage: This is used as a warning against talkativeness or trying too hard to impress others with speech.
igbo: A chọwa mma ekwu, e kwuo ihe eriri n'abalị

meaning: Persistent persecution or adversity can inadvertently drive a person to find success and a better life elsewhere.
literal: If one keeps chasing a person, one chases them into a good world.
usage: This is used to console someone undergoing persecution, reminding them that their trials may lead to a better future.
igbo: A chụkata mmadụ, a chụnye ya n'ụwa ọma

meaning: When a natural, expected outcome fails to happen, it is a sign that there is a serious underlying problem.
literal: If a sacrifice is offered and vultures are not seen, it is known that something happened in the land of the spirits.
usage: This is used to express concern when a routine event or expected response fails to occur, indicating a deeper issue.
igbo: A chụọ aja ahụghi udele amara na ihe mere n'ala ndị mmụọ

meaning: Just because a bad practice has gone on for a long time does not make it right or acceptable.
literal: One should not, because an evil thing has lasted a year, call it a tradition.
usage: This is used as a rebuke against defending corrupt or harmful practices simply because they have a long history.
igbo: A gaghị asị maka na ihe ọjọọ gbara afọ kpọọ ya omenaala

meaning: One should not use a remedy that is more destructive than the problem itself.
literal: One should not, because of an itch, scratch out one's eye.
usage: This is used as a warning to someone who is reacting too drastically to a minor annoyance or problem.
equivalent: The remedy is worse than the disease
igbo: A gaghị eji na ọkọ kọrọ wee kọpịa anya

meaning: One should not overindulge or spoil a child or dependent out of affection, to the point of ruining them.
literal: I will not, because my father reincarnated through me, choke him to death with food.
usage: This is used by a parent or guardian to justify disciplining or setting boundaries for a beloved child.
igbo: A gaghị m ekworo na nna m lọọrọ m ụwa nyegbue ya na nri

meaning: After all the excitement, celebrations, or temporary activities, things must eventually return to their normal, fundamental state.
literal: When the dance is finished, it returns to the waist.
usage: This is used to remind people to prepare for normal life after a major festival, event, or period of excitement.
igbo: A gbacha egwu, ọ laa n'ukwu

meaning: At the end of any endeavor, it is the actual results and achievements that will be measured and judged.
literal: After running, the miles are counted.
usage: This is used to remind someone that ultimate success is measured by final results, not just the effort expended along the way.
equivalent: The end crowns the work
igbo: A gbachaa ọsọ, agụọ mile

meaning: When there is unity of purpose and agreement among a group, even the most difficult or taboo tasks can be accomplished.
literal: If people agree on how to eat the vulture, the basket is lowered.
usage: This is used to encourage consensus and collective agreement before embarking on a challenging community project.
igbo: A gbakọọ ka aha eri udele, a tọtuo ngịga

meaning: When a person's primary source of hope or dependent is destroyed, they lose their reason to stay and will depart.
literal: If the baby bird is shot, its mother flies away.
usage: This is used to explain why someone abandoned a cause or a place after suffering a devastating personal loss.
igbo: A gbakwaa nwa nnụnụ, nne ya efelaga

meaning: While idle people waste time arguing over resources, the prepared and industrious person is already putting them to productive use.
literal: While people with empty hands are disputing land, the one who has seed yams is planting them.
usage: This is used as a rebuke to those who engage in endless disputes instead of doing productive work.
igbo: A gbara aka na-azọ ala, onye ji a na-akọ ji

meaning: If you neglect your health and well-being in a relentless pursuit of riches, you will die early and leave your wealth to those who do not care for you.
literal: If one ignores life to gather wealth, an enemy will consume it.
usage: This is used as a warning to workaholics to take care of their health and enjoy life rather than just hoarding wealth.
igbo: A ghara ndụ kpaa akụ, onye iro erie ya

meaning: No one can survive or succeed entirely on their own; we all need the support of a community.
literal: If a person is left alone, their world will crush them.
usage: This is used to emphasize the necessity of communal support and helping those who are struggling alone.
equivalent: No man is an island
igbo: A ghaara otu onye, ụwa ya anyịgbuo ya

meaning: One cannot endlessly plead innocence or make excuses; eventually, action must be taken, or consequences faced.
literal: If one prays with the staff of justice forever, the spirits will become deaf.
usage: This is used as a warning to someone who constantly makes excuses or delays taking responsibility for their actions.
igbo: A gọwa ọfọ ebighi ebi, nti echie ndi mmụọ

meaning: Even when a person reforms or recovers from a major flaw, some lingering traces of their old habits or character will always remain.
literal: Even if a madman is completely cured, his habit of muttering to himself cannot be cured.
usage: This is used to advise caution when dealing with a reformed person, reminding others that old habits die hard.
igbo: A gwọchagodi onye ara, anaghị agwọta ya ntakwu

meaning: No one can survive or succeed entirely on their own; we all need the support of a community.
literal: If a person is left alone, their world will crush them.
usage: This is used to emphasize the necessity of communal support and helping those who are struggling alone.
equivalent: No man is an island
igbo: A haara otu onye, ụwa ya anyịgbuo ya

meaning: It is foolish to ignore the actual source of a problem and instead direct one's anger or blame at an innocent or irrelevant party.
literal: If one leaves the buttocks that farted and punches the head.
usage: This is used as a rebuke to someone who is misdirecting their anger or blaming the wrong person for a mishap.
igbo: A hapụ ike nyụrụ ahụrụ ekee isi ọkpọ

meaning: A person's prominent status or greatness comes with visible, unavoidable flaws or heavy responsibilities.
literal: When a great man is seen, his long nose is also seen.
usage: This is used to remind people that even highly respected individuals have their own peculiar faults or burdens.
igbo: A hụ dimkpa, ahụ ogologo imi ya

meaning: A situation that is already bad is being made to seem catastrophically worse by unnecessary panic.
literal: One is consulting the oracle about hunger, and it is sounding like death.
usage: Used to caution someone against exaggerating a minor crisis or making a bad situation seem hopeless.
igbo: A na-agba afa na agụọ, ọ na-ada ọnwụ ọnwụ

meaning: Some things are so obviously harmful that one should not need to be warned against doing them.
literal: One warns the eye-paint that pepper is not put in it.
usage: Used as a rebuke to someone who is about to do something obviously self-destructive or foolish.
igbo: A na-agwa odo anya anaghị etinye ya ose

meaning: A situation where the remedy is making things worse, or escaping one trouble only to fall into a bigger one.
literal: While he is being treated for hernia, his belly is swelling.
usage: Used to lament a situation where attempts to solve a problem only result in a bigger, more complicated issue.
equivalent: Out of the frying pan into the fire
igbo: A na-agwọ ya ibi ya na-eto afọ

meaning: People who are sensitive or guilty often feel personally targeted when general examples are given.
literal: When the buttocks are used as an example, it feels as if it is in slavery.
usage: Used to mock or rebuke someone who unnecessarily takes a general remark or warning personally.
equivalent: If the shoe fits, wear it
igbo: A na-ama atụ otule, ọ dịka ọ nọ n'oru

meaning: One should prepare for an event based on the clear signs and warnings that precede it.
literal: One knows the state of water by its rain.
usage: Used to advise someone to take precautions when they see warning signs of trouble ahead.
equivalent: Forewarned is forearmed
igbo: A na-ama ọkwa mmiri maka ozuzo ya

meaning: It is better to be a living coward than a dead hero.
literal: One stands in the house of a coward to point at the house of the dead hero.
usage: Used to justify taking a cautious, safe approach to danger rather than risking one's life needlessly.
equivalent: Discretion is the better part of valor
igbo: A na-anọ be onye ụjọ atụ aka be dike

meaning: There is no need to fear someone's intimidating appearance or reputation when they ultimately cannot harm you.
literal: One is afraid of a woman with big hips, is she going to climb herself?
usage: Used to reassure someone not to be intimidated by a formidable-looking opponent or obstacle.
igbo: A na-atụ nwaanyị ike ukwu ụjọ, ọ bụ ya ga-arigo onwe ya?

meaning: Some forces or truths are completely unstoppable, no matter how much effort is made to suppress them.
literal: While the flood is being blocked, it breaks through.
usage: Used to acknowledge the futility of trying to suppress the truth or stop an inevitable change.
igbo: A na-egbochi ideyi, ọ na awa

meaning: When disaster strikes a close associate or relative, one cannot remain indifferent or happy, as they might be next.
literal: When the ram is being slaughtered, the ewe does not look happy.
usage: Used to express sympathy or solidarity when a neighbor or relative suffers a misfortune.
igbo: A na-egbu ebila ihu anaghị adị atụrụ mma

meaning: Resilient people or things thrive and multiply despite constant persecution or setbacks.
literal: As the elephant grass is being cut, it keeps growing.
usage: Used to praise someone's resilience or to declare that an unstoppable movement cannot be suppressed.
igbo: A na-egbu achara ọ na-eto

meaning: Life goes on with its essential, serious processes regardless of people's frivolous or vulgar distractions.
literal: While dancing and touching the vagina, the dead are reincarnating.
usage: Used to remind people that serious matters of life and destiny continue uninterrupted by superficial human activities.
igbo: A na-egwu egwu na ebisa aka na ikpu, ndị nwụrụ anwụ a na-alọ ụwa

meaning: Delicate matters must be handled with extreme care and patience to avoid causing harm.
literal: One gently scrapes the lice from the eyebrow.
usage: Used to advise someone to exercise patience and gentleness when dealing with a highly sensitive situation.
igbo: A na-eji nwayọ akọ ụkọ n'iku anya

meaning: Someone who is already in a bad or compromised situation goes ahead to make it worse by their own foolish actions.
literal: While people are saying that the chicken has feces on its leg, it goes ahead to peck it with its beak.
usage: Used to criticize someone who worsens their own bad reputation or plight through self-destructive behavior.
igbo: A na-ekwu na ọkụkọ bu nshị na okpa, o jiri ọnụ tụrụ ya

meaning: Troubles are multiplying when we already have more than enough to deal with.
literal: While we are saying that diseases are not enough, those with hernia are developing swollen bellies.
usage: Used to lament a succession of misfortunes or a situation that keeps getting progressively worse.
equivalent: When it rains, it pours
igbo: A na-ekwu na ọrịa ezughị oke, ndị dara ibi na-eto afọ

meaning: Asking redundant or foolishly detailed questions about an obviously disastrous or complete situation.
literal: While people are saying that the Reverend Father is naked, you are asking if his pubic hair is also showing.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who asks silly, obvious, or inappropriate questions when a major crisis is already clear.
igbo: A na-ekwu n'ụkọ gbara Father, ị na-ajụ ma ọ gbakwara ahụ ọnụ ya

meaning: [uncertain] While trying to build or beautify something, decay or counterproductive forces are simultaneously at work.
literal: While making brass, one is also making rust.
usage: Used to express frustration when progress is constantly being undermined by decay or setbacks.
igbo: A na-eme ọna a na-eme ọnammiri

meaning: People often take the kindness of those who love them and bestow it upon those they themselves desire, showing misplaced appreciation.
literal: While favors are being done for a young maiden, she is doing favors for the one she fancies.
usage: Used to complain about unrequited affection or when someone takes your generosity for granted to please someone else.
igbo: A na-emere agbọghọ, ya na-emere onye dị ya mma

meaning: A person's future potential, character, and greatness can be seen in their early actions and habits.
literal: It is from childhood that one knows the child who will slaughter a cow for his father's funeral.
usage: Used to praise a promising young person or to note that early signs indicate future success.
equivalent: The child is father of the man
igbo: A na-esi na nwata amara nwa ga-egburu nna ya ehi

meaning: Good behavior, reputation, and success begin at home before they are exhibited in public.
literal: It is from a beautiful home that one goes out to the public square.
usage: Used to emphasize the importance of proper upbringing and domestic stability as the foundation for public success.
equivalent: Charity begins at home
igbo: A na-esi n'ụlọ mara mma pụọ ama

meaning: One should not be overly greedy or try to do too many things at once.
literal: One does not put both hands into the mouth at the same time.
usage: Used to caution someone against greed, impatience, or taking on more than they can handle.
equivalent: Don't bite off more than you can chew
igbo: A naghị achịnye aka abụọ na ọnụ

meaning: Do not go looking for trouble or interfere in the affairs of someone who is already busy or desperate.
literal: One does not look for what is troubling someone who is looking for something.
usage: This is used to warn someone against meddling in another person's difficult business or provoking someone who is already stressed.
igbo: A naghị achọ ihe na-akpa onye na-achọ ihe

meaning: A person of noble character or high status is easily distinguished and does not need to be searched for among the common crowd.
literal: One does not search for a prince in the public square.
usage: This is used to praise someone's obvious nobility, outstanding character, or distinctiveness in a crowd.
igbo: A naghị achọ nwa eze achọ n'ọgbọ ọha

meaning: Important milestones or honorable people should not be approached without a token of respect or a gift.
literal: One does not see a child's tooth empty-handed.
usage: This is used to remind someone of the cultural obligation to bring a gift when visiting a newborn or celebrating a milestone.
igbo: A naghi agba aka ahụ nwata eze

meaning: One should not embark on a difficult, rare, or highly rewarding venture without proper preparation and tools.
literal: One does not climb an iroko tree empty-handed.
usage: This is used to advise someone to prepare adequately before undertaking a major task or visiting an influential person.
igbo: A naghị agba aka arị ọjị

meaning: Do not lose sight of the forest for the trees.
literal: One does not wear an ornament on the wrist and leave the thumb.
usage: This is used to rebuke someone who is focusing on minor details while ignoring the main issue.
equivalent: Don't lose sight of the forest for the trees.
igbo: A naghi agba ụria aka hapụ isi aka

meaning: Don't cross your bridges before you come to them.
literal: One does not spit for feces that is still in the stomach.
usage: This is used to advise someone to stop worrying about or reacting to a future problem that hasn't happened yet.
equivalent: Don't cross your bridges before you come to them.
igbo: A naghị agbara nshị nọ n'afọ asụ

meaning: Don't teach your grandmother to suck eggs.
literal: One does not tell a wine-tapper that there is work in tapping the raffia palm.
usage: This is used to rebuke someone who is presumptuously offering advice to an experienced professional.
equivalent: Don't teach your grandmother to suck eggs.
igbo: A naghị agwa diochi na ọrụ di na ngwọ

meaning: There is no need to explain the obvious to someone who can easily perceive it themselves.
literal: One does not tell a blind person that there is no salt in the soup.
usage: This is used to point out that a situation is so obvious that it requires no further explanation or discussion.
igbo: A naghị agwa onye isi na nnu adịghị n’ofe

meaning: Some situations are so obvious or inevitable that even the most oblivious person will eventually realize them without being told.
literal: One does not tell a deaf person that the market has dispersed.
usage: This is used to warn someone that they cannot ignore a glaring reality or impending consequence for long.
igbo: A naghi agwa oshi ntị na ahịa esula

meaning: Do not abandon a prestigious, honorable, or highly beneficial opportunity to pursue a troublesome or lesser affair.
literal: One does not leave where an Ozo title is being conferred to go where Agwu is being appeased.
usage: This is used to advise someone to prioritize noble and constructive endeavors over chaotic or unproductive ones.
igbo: A naghi ahapụ ebe ana-echi ọzọ jebe ebe a na arụ agwụ

meaning: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
literal: One does not leave the thumb to wear a ring on the pinky.
usage: This is used to warn someone against abandoning a secure and important relationship or asset for something trivial.
equivalent: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
igbo: A naghị ahapụ isiaka were agba ụrịọm

meaning: Do not seek unnecessary assistance or delay action when the path forward is already perfectly clear.
literal: One does not see the road clearly and then ask for a light to be lit.
usage: This is used to urge someone to take action immediately since there are no obstacles or ambiguities remaining.
igbo: A naghị ahụcha ụzọ sị mụta okụ

meaning: Don't look a gift horse in the mouth.
literal: One does not reject food that is covered.
usage: This is used to advise someone to accept a well-intentioned offer or gift with gratitude.
equivalent: Don't look a gift horse in the mouth.
igbo: A naghị ajụ nri ekpusiri ekpusi

meaning: Do not reject a complete, well-presented offer or a package deal that comes with all its necessary parts.
literal: One does not reject a plate and its lid.
usage: This is used to encourage someone to accept a generous, complete offer or a wholesome package without complaints.
igbo: A naghị ajụ efere na nkwuchi

meaning: Do not fuss over minor details or personal choices of an independent person as long as the ultimate, successful outcome is achieved.
literal: One does not ask a bachelor where he slept the night; what is more important is whether he returned.
usage: This is used to advise against micromanaging or questioning the methods of an independent agent when the final result is satisfactory.
igbo: A naghị ajụ okokporo ebe ọ rahụrụ ụra na abalị, ihe ka mkpa bụ ma ọ lọtarakwara

meaning: You cannot have your cake and eat it too.
literal: One does not hold water in the mouth and blow the fire.
usage: This is used to warn someone that they must choose one path because they cannot successfully do two conflicting things at once.
equivalent: You cannot have your cake and eat it too.
igbo: A naghị akpụ mmiri n'ọnụ afụ okụ

meaning: Don't cast pearls before swine.
literal: One does not wash hands just to crack palm kernels for a chicken.
usage: This is used to advise someone against over-preparing or wasting valuable resources on an unworthy recipient or minor task.
equivalent: Don't cast pearls before swine.
igbo: A naghị akwọ aka etiri ọkụkọ akị

meaning: You can't teach an old dog new tricks.
literal: One does not learn to be left-handed in old age.
usage: This is used to explain why an older person is resistant to changing their long-held habits or lifestyle.
equivalent: You can't teach an old dog new tricks.
igbo: A naghị amụ aka ekpe na nka

meaning: Don't dig your well when you are thirsty.
literal: One does not stand at the battlefront to sharpen arrows.
usage: This is used to rebuke someone for failing to prepare beforehand and trying to make hasty preparations in the middle of an emergency.
equivalent: Don't dig your well when you are thirsty.
igbo: A naghị anọ n'ihu ọgụ apị akụ

meaning: To fully understand a situation or succeed in life, one must be dynamic, adaptable, and willing to view things from different perspectives.
literal: One does not stand in one place to watch a masquerade.
usage: This is used to encourage someone to travel, change their approach, or seek new perspectives rather than remaining stagnant.
igbo: A naghị anọ ofu ebe ekiri mmanwụ

meaning: One should avoid unnecessary danger and keep quiet when in the presence of terrifying or supernatural forces.
literal: One does not smell the breath of the spirits and keep one's mouth wide open.
usage: Used as a warning to someone who is behaving recklessly in a highly dangerous situation.
igbo: A naghị anụ isi ndi mmụọ ghewe ọnụ oghe

meaning: Do not interfere with or dictate the private habits of elders, as they have reasons for their actions that you may not understand.
literal: One does not tell an old woman to close her legs together, as one does not know where she breathes from.
usage: Used to caution someone against questioning or trying to regulate the unconventional behavior of an elder.
igbo: A naghị asi agadị nwaanyị mechikụlọta ụkwụ, a maghị ebe o si eku ume

meaning: Respect the autonomy of elders; they are wise enough to know what is good for them and do not need to be told the obvious.
literal: One does not tell an elder to get out of the sun.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who is trying to patronize or give unnecessary advice to an older, wiser person.
igbo: A naghị asị okenye pụta n'anwụ

meaning: You cannot hide an activity that by its very nature makes a lot of noise or attracts attention.
literal: One does not chew crab bones in secret.
usage: Used to warn someone that their secret plans or illicit activities will inevitably be exposed.
igbo: A naghị ata okpụkpụ nshịkọ na nzuzo

meaning: A fair judgment cannot be made without hearing both sides of the story.
literal: One does not settle a dispute by hearing only one voice.
usage: Used by a mediator or judge to insist on hearing from the accused before making a decision.
equivalent: There are two sides to every story
igbo: A naghị ebi ikpe n'otu olu

meaning: You cannot expect good results from an entirely different or unsuitable source.
literal: One does not harvest breadfruit from an oil bean tree.
usage: Used to point out the futility of expecting a certain quality or behavior from someone whose nature or background is completely different.
equivalent: You cannot gather grapes from thorns
igbo: A naghi ebute ụkwa n'osisi ụkpaka

meaning: Do not give someone a task and then simultaneously create obstacles that make it impossible for them to succeed.
literal: One does not ask a child to fetch fire and then pour water on them.
usage: Used to protest against contradictory demands or unfair sabotage by a superior.
igbo: A naghi edinye nwata mụta ọkụ, hakwasị ya mmiri

meaning: Do not undermine or ruin the very task you have assigned someone to do.
literal: One does not send a child on an errand to fetch salt and then pour water on them.
usage: Used to criticize a leader or parent who sabotages their own instructions or subordinates.
igbo: A naghi edinye nwata ozi nnụ, hakwasị ya mmiri

meaning: Do not expose valuable assets to obvious temptation or danger.
literal: One does not lead a goat to the yam barn.
usage: Used as a warning against putting someone in a position where they will easily be tempted to steal or cause damage.
equivalent: Do not put the fox in charge of the henhouse
igbo: A naghi edu ewu eje n'ọba

meaning: Do not make critical decisions or assessments when you lack clear information or when conditions are unfavorable.
literal: One does not use the night to measure distance with the eyes.
usage: Used to advise someone to postpone a decision until they have better visibility or more facts.
igbo: A naghị eji abalị arọ anya

meaning: You must be extremely alert and sharp when dealing with someone who is exceptionally clever or vigilant.
literal: One does not go to the squirrel's house with blurry eyes, because the squirrel is all eyes.
usage: Used to warn someone to be fully prepared and cautious when negotiating with a shrewd opponent.
igbo: A naghị eji anya nchakasị aga na nke atanị, maka atanị bụ anya anya

meaning: Do not apply a solution meant for one specific problem to a completely different and sensitive situation.
literal: One does not put what is meant for the ear into the eye.
usage: Used to caution someone against using inappropriate methods or tools for a delicate task.
igbo: A naghị eji ihe ana-agba na ntị agba n'anya

meaning: Do not let politeness or embarrassment prevent you from protecting your own life, health, or well-being.
literal: One does not swallow poison out of shyness.
usage: Used to encourage someone to speak up or refuse a harmful request, even if doing so feels socially awkward.
igbo: A naghị eji ihere elo anwa

meaning: If you have all the necessary resources or support, you should not have to suffer or struggle needlessly.
literal: One does not have a complete set of drums and still beat one's chest.
usage: Used to remind someone to utilize the abundant resources or helpers available to them instead of struggling in vain.
igbo: A naghị enwecha nkwa, na-akwa aka n'ume

meaning: Do not entrust valuable things to someone who is bound by their nature to consume or abuse them.
literal: One does not give a bone to a dog and tell it to guard it.
usage: Used to criticize or warn against a foolish delegation of duty to an untrustworthy person.
equivalent: Do not put the fox in charge of the henhouse
igbo: A naghị enye nkịta ọkpụkpọ sị ya chebe

meaning: Do not try to cheat or sell defective goods to people who live close to you, as your deception will quickly be discovered.
literal: One does not sell a short-legged chicken nearby.
usage: Used to warn someone against dishonest dealings within their own community or immediate circle.
igbo: A naghị ere ọkụkọ ụkwụ mkpirisi na nso

meaning: Do not inflict excessive punishment or strip someone of their dignity while correcting them.
literal: One does not beat a child and also take away their clothes.
usage: Used to plead for mercy or to rebuke someone who is being overly harsh and vindictive in punishing an offender.
igbo: A naghị eti nwata ihe nara ya akwa

meaning: Discipline is more effective when administered calmly and deliberately, rather than in the heat of anger over a costly accident.
literal: One does not beat a child on the day they spill palm oil, but rather on the day they spill oil-palm dregs.
usage: Used to advise a parent or leader to exercise restraint and not let anger over a material loss dictate their disciplinary actions.
igbo: A naghị eti nwata ihe ụbọchị ọ wụfuru mmanụ ka ma ọ bụ ụbọchị ọ wụfuru ogiri akwụ

meaning: Do not pick a fight with someone who has strong backing and community support.
literal: I do not beat a masquerade that is being pushed or supported by others.
usage: Used by a speaker to explain why they are avoiding a confrontation with a well-connected opponent.
igbo: A naghị m eti mmọnwụ a na-akwa aka

meaning: An injury or injustice done to one member of a group affects the security and well-being of the entire community.
literal: If fish is taken from one fisherman, it has been taken from his companion.
usage: Used to rally solidarity and collective action when a member of a community is mistreated by an outsider.
equivalent: An injury to one is an injury to all
igbo: A nara ofu onye oru azụ, a narago ibe ya

meaning: Desperate times call for desperate measures.
literal: When one sees something greater than the farm, one sells the barn.
usage: A speaker uses this to justify making an extreme sacrifice or selling off valuable assets to handle an unprecedented crisis.
equivalent: Desperate times call for desperate measures.
igbo: A hụ ihe ka ubi e ree ọba

meaning: When you lack the means to achieve a goal, opportunities or demands seem to mock you by appearing everywhere.
literal: When there is no money to marry a wife for the first son, all pregnant women seem to be giving birth to boys.
usage: This is used as a lament or observation when one is financially constrained and unable to meet pressing social expectations.
igbo: A hụghị ego lụnye ọkpara nwaanyị ụmụ nwaanyị niile di ime a na-mụ nwoke nwoke

meaning: If you cannot do things the ideal way, you must adapt and do the best you can with what is available.
literal: If one does not see how it is done, one does as one sees.
usage: This is used to encourage adaptability and pragmatism when resources or ideal conditions are lacking.
igbo: A hụghị ka e mere, e mee ka a hụrụ

meaning: Reckless behavior or consuming things blindly without investigation leads to sudden and unexpected ruin.
literal: Eating without asking causes dying without falling sick.
usage: This serves as a stern warning against accepting gifts, food, or deals blindly without verifying their source or safety.
igbo: A jụghị ajụ eri na-ebute arịaghị arịa anwụ

meaning: [uncertain] One should not presumptuously offer or force pre-determined terms on others without consulting them first.
literal: I did not ask whether it is peeled, I am selling it peeled.
usage: This is used to rebuke someone who acts presumptuously or makes decisions on behalf of others without their consent.
igbo: A jụghị m ma akpọwara m akpọwa ka m na-ere ere

meaning: Hard work and suffering in the present lead to comfort and enjoyment in the future.
literal: If one plants in the sun, one eats in the shade.
usage: This is used to encourage someone undergoing hard labor or difficult studies to persevere for future rewards.
equivalent: No pain, no gain.
igbo: A kọọ n'anwu, e rie na ndụ

meaning: Every story or matter must be fully heard and understood before a judgment can be made.
literal: When it is narrated to the end, it will be listened to the end.
usage: This is used as a call for patience and a fair hearing during a dispute or when listening to a complex explanation.
igbo: A kọruo e geruo

meaning: Despite grand plans, elaborate preparations, or high status, one must ultimately return to simple realities or accept one's basic human limitations.
literal: After all the discussions and plans, one still sleeps on a mat.
usage: This serves as a sobering reminder to remain humble or to accept that elaborate schemes often end in simple, practical realities.
igbo: A kpaa akpaa a rahụọ n'ute

meaning: [uncertain] It is foolish to worry about minor details or secondary preparations when the primary, essential task has not even been started.
literal: Has medicine been prepared, let alone the pad for carrying it?
usage: This is used to rebuke someone who is prematurely focusing on the rewards or minor details of a project that has not yet begun.
equivalent: Don't put the cart before the horse.
igbo: A kụla ọgwụ, ọ bụ ma ajụ?

meaning: When a formal call to action or emergency is sounded, the community must gather to respond.
literal: When the wooden drum is beaten, the public square fills up.
usage: This is used to emphasize the duty of citizens to assemble and take collective action when summoned by leadership.
igbo: A kụọ ekwe ama agbaa

meaning: Encroaching on another person's territory or rights will inevitably provoke a conflict.
literal: When the boundary wall is pushed, a fight is seen.
usage: This serves as a warning to someone who is pushing boundaries or provoking another, signaling that their actions will lead to retaliation.
igbo: A kwaa aja a hụ ọgụ

meaning: Even the strongest or most patient person will eventually break, lose confidence, or become intimidated if subjected to relentless pressure.
literal: If a brave man is repeatedly pushed on the chest, fear is instilled in him.
usage: This is used as a warning against pushing someone too far, or as an explanation of why a strong person has finally shown weakness.
igbo: A kwakata dike aka n'obi, a kwanye ya ụjọ

meaning: Taking shortcuts or refusing to humble oneself initially only results in double the work and effort later on.
literal: If one stands upright and breaks the yam while digging, one must bend down to dig out its tail.
usage: This is used to rebuke someone who tried to do a job lazily or half-heartedly and now has to spend extra effort correcting their mistake.
equivalent: Haste makes waste.
igbo: A kwụrụ ọtọ gwujie ji, ehulọta gwuputa ọdụ ya

meaning: People easily discard old, loyal friends or reliable tools as soon as they acquire something new and attractive.
literal: When a young bride is married, the old woman is cast out.
usage: This is used to critique human fickleness and ingratitude when someone abandons their old associates for new ones.
equivalent: Out with the old, in with the new.
igbo: A lụta agbọghọ, a chụpụ agadị

meaning: One must distinguish between major, significant events and minor, inconsequential ones.
literal: One knows the rain that fell, and also knows the one that merely drizzled.
usage: This is used to advise someone to prioritize their concerns or to recognize the difference between a serious threat and a minor nuisance.
igbo: A ma mmiri zoro ozo, mara nke tasara atasa

meaning: [uncertain] One cannot expect to preserve or store away resources when they are already being greedily consumed as fast as they are gathered.
literal: While one is gathering fire and licking one's fingers, will it be hung on the ceiling shelf?
usage: This is used to rebuke someone who is consuming their capital or resources immediately instead of saving them for the future.
equivalent: You cannot have your cake and eat it too.
igbo: A na-achi ọkụ aracha aka, a ga-ekonye ya n'uko

meaning: Wise people learn from the advice, corrections, or misfortunes directed at others.
literal: While the child who has a mother is being advised, the motherless child listens in.
usage: This is used to encourage onlookers to pay attention to a lesson being taught to someone else, so they can benefit from it too.
equivalent: A word to the wise is sufficient.
igbo: A na-adụ nwa nwere nne ọdụ nke na enweghi nne na-egere

meaning: An unrepentant wrongdoer will pretend to listen to advice while secretly planning their next crime.
literal: While a yam thief is being advised, he is mentally sharpening his digging stick.
usage: This is used as a cynical observation about a stubborn or deceitful person who refuses to reform despite receiving counsel.
igbo: A na-adụ onye oshi ji ọdụ, ya were obi na-apịa mbazụ

meaning: The true value of social gatherings and community events is the human connection and fellowship, not the physical setting itself.
literal: People go to the moonlight play to see other people, not to see the moon, because the moon shines in everyone's home.
usage: This is used to emphasize the importance of community, solidarity, and social interaction over material or environmental factors.
igbo: A na-aga egwu ọnwa ka ahụ mmadụ ọ bụghị ka ahụ ọnwa, maka ọnwa na-eti n'ụlọ onye ọbụla

meaning: The primary purpose of travel and exposure to other cultures is to gain wisdom and experience, not merely to seek material comfort or luxury.
literal: One travels to other lands to learn things, not to fill one's belly.
usage: This is used to advise a traveler or student abroad to focus on self-improvement, education, and cultural exchange rather than physical indulgence.
igbo: A na-aga mba ka amụta ihe ọ bụghị ka e rijue afọ

meaning: A guilty person takes extreme precautions to hide their tracks or protect themselves from the consequences of their actions.
literal: The cricket knows what it did and blocked its hole and blocked its whiskers.
usage: This is used to mock or point out someone who is acting defensively because they have a guilty conscience.
igbo: Abụzụ maara ihe o mere gbachie ụpụ gbachie isi ọnụ

meaning: When ideal options or support are unavailable, one must make do with what is closest and most practical.
literal: If one keeps looking for where to rest one's hand, one rests it on the knee.
usage: This is used to advise someone to accept a practical, readily available alternative when their preferred choices fail.
igbo: Achọgide ebe a ga ebido aka, ebido n'ikpere

meaning: The necessity of earning a living and feeding oneself keeps a person constantly working and moving.
literal: The stomach does not allow the feet to rest.
usage: This is used to explain or lament the relentless need to work daily to survive.
igbo: Afọ ekweghi ụkwụ zuo ike

meaning: Excessive generosity or kindness can sometimes lead to one's own ruin or poverty.
literal: Generosity and crawling on the ground.
usage: This is used as a warning against being overly generous to the point of self-sabotage.
equivalent: No good deed goes unpunished
igbo: Afọ ọma ya na akpụ n'ala

meaning: The world keeps moving and community life continues regardless of the absence or loss of a single individual.
literal: The Umuduru market day does not know that one person did not come to the market.
usage: This is used to humble someone who thinks their absence will disrupt a group's activities.
igbo: Afọ Umuduru amaghị na ofu onye abiaghị ahịa

meaning: One never loses their mastery or passion for a skill they have practiced and perfected over a lifetime.
literal: An old woman does not grow too old for a dance she knows how to dance.
usage: This is used to express confidence in someone's enduring ability to perform a task they are highly experienced in.
equivalent: You never forget how to ride a bicycle
igbo: Agadi nwaanyị anaghị aka nka n'egwu ọ ma agba

meaning: Experiencing repeated failures or misfortunes forces a person to re-evaluate their situation and take stock of their mistakes.
literal: If an old woman falls twice, she counts what she is carrying in her basket.
usage: This is used to advise someone to pause and reflect on their strategy after suffering consecutive setbacks.
igbo: Agadi nwaanyị daa ada ugboro abụọ, ọ gụọ ihe o bu n'ísi ọnụ

meaning: Making unnecessary excuses or finding fault in a simple task when one is merely asked to help in a basic way.
literal: An old woman is handed a baby to hold, and she complains that she has no teeth, as if she was expected to bite the baby to death.
usage: This is used to rebuke someone who makes absurd, defensive excuses to avoid doing a simple favor.
igbo: Agadi nwaanyị e kunyere nwa, ọ sị ya enwezighi eze, a sọ ya tagbuo ya atagbu

meaning: While one person is planning to exploit or enjoy something, the object or other person is simultaneously planning their undoing.
literal: The old woman is planning how to eat the spinach, while the spinach is planning how to give the old woman diarrhea.
usage: This is used as a warning that an apparently easy target or opportunity may have hidden, harmful consequences.
igbo: Agadi nwaanyị na-eche ka ọ ga-esi ri inine, inine a na-eche ka ọga-esi saa nwaanyị afọ

meaning: When people are well-supported and cared for, they do not feel the harsh burdens of aging or hardship.
literal: An old person who has someone taking care of them says that their lineage does not grow old.
usage: This is used to highlight the importance of family support and care in making life easier for the vulnerable.
igbo: Agadi nwere onye na-elekọta ya, sị na agbụrụ ya anaghị aka nka

meaning: Refusing to walk blindly into a pre-arranged trap or a situation where the outcome has already been unfairly decided against you.
literal: I will not enter a barn where cocoyams are already tied.
usage: This is used to assert one's independence and refusal to participate in a rigged setup or conspiracy.
igbo: Agaghị m aba n'ọba e kere ede

meaning: To resolve a persistent problem, one must block all escape routes or address the root loophole.
literal: If the backyard path is not blocked, the wrestling match does not end.
usage: This is used to advise taking decisive action to close loopholes in order to finally settle a dispute or problem.
igbo: Agbaghị ụzọ owerre mgba ọnaghị eshi

meaning: A person who is too impatient or proud to accept reasonable offers or compromises will eventually have to settle for something much worse.
literal: A deity that runs away from sacrifices ends up eating a bad goat.
usage: This is used to warn someone against being overly picky or rejecting good gestures, lest they end up with nothing.
igbo: Agbara na-agba ọsọ aja, na-eri ewu ọjọọ

meaning: In times of extreme necessity or crisis, one must make do with whatever imperfect resources are available.
literal: If the shallow water is stirred up and muddy, one still scoops and drinks it.
usage: This is used to justify using less-than-ideal resources or accepting flawed solutions when there is no other choice.
equivalent: Beggars can't be choosers
igbo: Agbarụọ ngele e kuru ṅụọ

meaning: The people who live closest to you are your most immediate source of help and solidarity, often more so than distant relatives.
literal: One's neighbor is one's sibling.
usage: This is used to encourage good neighborly relations and mutual support within a local community.
igbo: Agbataobi onye bụ nwanne ya

meaning: Painful experiences and mistakes teach people to be more cautious and wise in the future.
literal: If a stinging ant bites the buttocks, it learns wisdom.
usage: This is used to explain how a painful lesson has made someone more careful, or to predict that a reckless person will learn from their mistakes.
equivalent: Once bitten, twice shy
igbo: Agbịsị gbaa otele ọ mụrụ akọ

meaning: No matter how fast or early one achieves success, they must eventually wait for others to catch up, as life has natural stages everyone goes through.
literal: When a young woman matures fully, she waits for her peers.
usage: This is used to counsel patience to those who are eager to rush ahead of their peers, reminding them that everyone eventually reaches the same milestones.
igbo: Agbọghọbịa tochaa o chere ibe ya

meaning: People who stand to benefit from your demise or failure cannot be trusted to help you recover or succeed.
literal: A lineage that inherits the estate of the deceased does not treat the sick person.
usage: This is used as a warning to avoid seeking help from those who have a conflict of interest or who profit from one's misfortune.
igbo: Agbụrụ na-eri ekpe anaghị agwọ onye ọrịa

meaning: Painful experiences and mistakes teach people to be more cautious and wise in the future.
literal: If a stinging ant bites the buttocks, it learns wisdom.
usage: This is used to explain how a painful lesson has made someone more careful, or to predict that a reckless person will learn from their mistakes.
equivalent: Once bitten, twice shy
igbo: Agbụsị gbaa otele ọ mụrụ akọ

meaning: When a danger or trouble is warned about well in advance, even the most vulnerable have enough time to prepare and escape.
literal: A war that is foretold does not consume a lame person.
usage: This is used to emphasize the value of early warnings, or to blame someone who suffered from a predictable disaster they were warned about.
equivalent: Forewarned is forearmed
igbo: Agha akara aka anaghị eri ngwọrọ

meaning: One should not compromise their dignity or perform degrading acts merely for financial gain.
literal: I am no longer dancing so that I can collect money.
usage: A declaration of self-respect by someone refusing to do a demeaning task for money.
igbo: A nazịghị m agba ka m data ego

meaning: It is inappropriate to bring up mystical, irrelevant, or out-of-place topics in a practical, everyday gathering.
literal: While sitting among humans, one speaks of spirits.
usage: A rebuke to someone who introduces inappropriate or distracting topics into a serious discussion.
igbo: A nọdị mmadụ mmadụ a na-ekwu mmụọ mmụọ

meaning: Change is inevitable over time, and one must adapt to changing circumstances.
literal: If one stays long enough, one shifts positions.
usage: A consolation or observation that difficult situations do not remain static forever.
igbo: A nọgide anọgharịa

meaning: When a person in authority makes an unexpected decision, it throws subordinates or common people into confusion.
literal: If one farts from a height, it confuses the flies.
usage: An observation on the chaotic ripple effect that the actions of leaders have on the masses.
igbo: A nọrọ n'elu nyụọ ahụrụ, ọgba ijiji gharịị

meaning: Life has a way of balancing things out, and persistent efforts will eventually yield diverse results.
literal: If one keeps marrying to bear a male child, one marries again and bears a female child.
usage: An encouragement to keep trying, reminding someone that persistence brings a full range of experiences.
igbo: A nụkata na-amụrụ nwoke a nụwa na-amụrụ nwaanyị

meaning: When people unite and work together, they can achieve great things that would be impossible individually.
literal: When people urinate together in one place, it foams.
usage: An exhortation to a community or family to work together to achieve a difficult goal.
equivalent: In unity lies strength
igbo: A nyụkọọ mamịrị ọnụ, ọ gba ụfụfụ

meaning: If one does not exercise self-control or set boundaries, things will quickly get out of hand.
literal: If one defecates without pinching the anus, it becomes diarrhea.
usage: A warning to someone to exercise restraint or discipline before a situation degenerates.
igbo: A nyụọ nshị akapịghị ọnụ, ọ bụrụ otoro

meaning: Hard work in the present leads to comfort and enjoyment in the future.
literal: If one works in the sun, one eats in the shade.
usage: An encouragement to someone undergoing hard labor, reminding them of the future rewards.
equivalent: No pain, no gain
igbo: A rụọ n'anwụ, e rie na ndụ

meaning: A guilty or deceitful person will always find absurd excuses to avoid doing what is right or being exposed.
literal: When a thief is asked to catch a chicken, he says it will bite him to death.
usage: A rebuke of someone making ridiculous excuses to avoid a simple duty or to hide their true nature.
igbo: A sị onye ohi nwude ọkụkọ ọ si na ọ ga-atagbu ya

meaning: People's judgment of goodness is subjective and naturally biased toward those who are close to them.
literal: If a child is asked to call a good person, they call their mother's friend.
usage: An observation about human bias and how people favor their own associates.
igbo: A sị nwata kpọọ onye ọma, ọ kpọọ enyi nne ya

meaning: When respect or fear of authority becomes too oppressive, people will find indirect or desperate ways to speak the truth.
literal: If one fears the king too much, one covers oneself with a basket to speak to him.
usage: A warning to a leader that excessive intimidation will only lead to anonymous or rebellious criticism.
igbo: A sọgide eze, ekpuru nkata gwa ya okwu

meaning: Life requires moderation, variety, or balancing different aspects of one's affairs.
literal: One chews a bit of breadfruit, then chews a bit of palm kernel.
usage: Advice to someone to balance their activities, diet, or resources rather than consuming or doing only one thing.
igbo: A tatụ ụkwa a tatụ akị

meaning: If you discard the core values or essential qualities that make you respected, you lose your worth.
literal: If that which makes something beautiful is thrown away, the beauty is ruined.
usage: A warning against abandoning one's cultural heritage, moral values, or unique strengths.
igbo: A tụfuo ihe e ji ama mma, mma arụọ

meaning: Do not discard old or seemingly useless things, as they may become indispensable in specific situations.
literal: If a tattered basket is thrown away, when the day of sacrifice arrives, it will be sought after.
usage: A warning against prematurely discarding old items or dismissing people who seem currently useless.
equivalent: Waste not, want not
igbo: A tụfuo nkịrịnka nkata, ubọchị a ga achụ aja ruo, a chọwa ya

meaning: A guilty or self-conscious person easily takes general remarks as personal insults.
literal: When a proverb about a tattered basket is spoken, the lean person's face spoils.
usage: Used to mock or point out someone who has reacted defensively to a general statement.
equivalent: If the shoe fits, wear it
igbo: A tụọ ilu nkịrịnka nkata, ihu agbajọọ onye tara ahụ

meaning: Wise people understand subtle hints and proverbs, while foolish people completely misunderstand them and act erratically.
literal: If a proverb is spoken to a wise person, they understand; if spoken to a fool, they run headlong into the bush.
usage: Used to praise someone who quickly understands a subtle hint, or to mock a fool who completely misses the point.
equivalent: A word to the wise is sufficient
igbo: A tụọrọ ọ mara ọ mara, a tụọrọ ofeke o fenye isi n'ọhịa

meaning: When offering help or a gift to someone who is defensive, make your good intentions clear to avoid misunderstanding.
literal: If one throws a bone to a puppy, one shows it to him, so he does not think you threw a stone at him.
usage: Advice on how to perform acts of charity or goodwill delicately without causing offense.
igbo: A tụpụ nwa nkịta igwi, egosi ya, ka ọ ghara iche na ị tụrụ ya mbọ

meaning: Proverbs serve as a coded language that only the wise can decode, leaving the foolish in the dark.
literal: Proverbs are spoken to confuse the fool.
usage: Used to justify speaking in riddles or coded language during a discussion to exclude undiscerning people.
igbo: A tụrụ ilu ka ọ gba ofeke gharịị

meaning: Dwelling too long on a minor grievance or trivial issue will only escalate it into a major conflict.
literal: If one keeps discussing the nature of a fart, it turns into feces.
usage: A warning to stop arguing over trivial matters before the situation gets out of hand.
igbo: A tụwa agwa ahụrụ a baa nshị

meaning: Preserving life is the ultimate priority; everything else can be dealt with later.
literal: If life is saved, death is set aside.
usage: Used to console someone who has lost property but survived a disaster, emphasizing that survival is what matters most.
equivalent: Where there's life, there's hope
igbo: A zọta ndu, edebere ọnwụ

meaning: When a powerful or dangerous person arrives, the weak or vulnerable must quickly scatter for their own safety.
literal: When the leopard enters, the antelope flees.
usage: This is used as a warning to weaker parties to avoid direct confrontation with a formidable opponent.
igbo: Agụ bata mgbada awara ọsọ

meaning: If a disaster or hardship can ruin those who are wealthy and well-prepared, it will completely devastate those who are poor and vulnerable.
literal: If hunger kills a rich man, when it gets to a poor man it tears him apart.
usage: This is used to warn of an impending crisis that will hit the most vulnerable members of society the hardest.
igbo: Agụọ gburu ogaranya nwete ogbenye ọ dọrie ya

meaning: Hardship is easy to endure when there is a reliable hope of relief in the near future.
literal: Hunger that has hope does not kill.
usage: This is used to console someone going through temporary hardship, encouraging them to hold on.
igbo: Agụọ nwere olile anya anaghị egbu egbu

meaning: Good character and natural beauty are most admirable when they are innate and genuine rather than artificial.
literal: Character is better when the python designs it.
usage: This is used to praise someone's natural, unpretentious good behavior or authentic beauty.
igbo: Agwa ka mma ma eke tụa ya

meaning: Children inevitably inherit the traits, behaviors, and characteristics of their parents.
literal: A snake must give birth to something with a long tail.
usage: This is used to comment on a child exhibiting the same behaviors, good or bad, as their parent.
equivalent: Like father, like son
igbo: Agwọ aghaghị imu ihe nwere ọdụ ogologo

meaning: There is a hidden danger or a treacherous person lurking in a seemingly safe or familiar place.
literal: There is a snake in the thatch.
usage: This is used as a warning to be cautious because of suspected hidden treachery or danger nearby.
equivalent: A snake in the grass
igbo: Agwọ dị n'akịrịka

meaning: If you do not assert your authority or defend your dignity, people will treat you with disrespect and take advantage of you.
literal: If a snake does not behave like a snake, children will use it to tie firewood.
usage: This is used to advise someone to assert themselves or show their strength so they are not taken for granted.
igbo: Agwọ emeghị ihe o ji bụrụ agwọ ụmụ aka ewere ya kee nkụ

meaning: A person who destroys or absorbs their peer or relative inherits double the trouble, complexity, or visibility.
literal: A snake that swallows its fellow snake has two tails.
usage: This is used to warn against greedily destroying one's own kind, as it brings unwanted complications.
igbo: Agwọ loro ibe ya na-enwe ọdụ abụọ

meaning: An unverified story or a danger witnessed by only one person is easily exaggerated.
literal: A snake seen by only one person becomes a python.
usage: This is used to express skepticism about an exaggerated report or rumor that lacks secondary witnesses.
igbo: Agwọ otu onye hụrụ na-aghọ eke

meaning: You cannot escape your destiny or avoid an inevitable confrontation, no matter how much you try to keep your distance.
literal: The snake says that if one's hand cannot reach it, one's foot will step on it.
usage: This is used to comment on an unavoidable encounter or a trouble that finds someone despite their precautions.
igbo: Agwọ sị onye aka ya na-ekotereghi ụkwụ ya ekotere ya

meaning: An attacker's efforts are wasted when they strike an opponent who is fully protected or has nothing to lose.
literal: The snake bit the tortoise, it bit an empty shell.
usage: This is used to mock an adversary's futile attempt to harm someone who is invulnerable or well-defended.
igbo: Agwọ tụrụ mbe, tụrụ okpokoro

meaning: My reputation is constantly being slandered by detractors behind my back.
literal: My name is never good in whispers.
usage: This is used to complain about being the constant target of malicious gossip or backbiting.
igbo: Aha m anaghị adị mma na mkporohihi

meaning: High-quality goods or genuine virtue do not need loud advertisement to be appreciated.
literal: A good market sells itself.
usage: This is used to praise something of obvious quality or a person of undeniable merit who does not boast.
equivalent: Good wine needs no bush
igbo: Ahịa dị mma na-ere onwe

meaning: When two equally cunning or stingy people try to outsmart each other, neither will make a profit.
literal: A trade between a tortoise and a tortoise yields no profit.
usage: This is used to describe a transaction or negotiation between two notoriously shrewd people where neither can gain an advantage.
igbo: Ahịa mbe na mbe na-azụ uru anaghị adị na ya

meaning: Excellent products or good deeds speak for themselves and require no self-promotion.
literal: A good market sells itself.
usage: This is used to emphasize that true value or talent will naturally attract recognition without boasting.
equivalent: Good wine needs no bush
igbo: Ahịa ọma na-ere onwe ya

meaning: Everyone prioritizes and understands best their own business, interests, or personal affairs.
literal: The market one buys from is what is clear to one's eyes.
usage: This is used to defend one's focus on their own affairs or to advise someone to mind their own business.
igbo: Ahịa onye na-azụ ka ọma anya ya

meaning: The true success, failure, or consequence of an enterprise can only be fully judged after it has come to an end.
literal: When the market finishes trading, its noise is heard.
usage: This is used to advise patience, reminding others to wait until an event is fully concluded before making a final judgment.
igbo: Ahịa zụchaa a nụ ụda ya

meaning: One should only commit resources or take action when the necessary preparation or reward is guaranteed.
literal: Upon seeing the soup, one pounds the fufu.
usage: This is used to justify waiting for concrete assurance or resources before starting a task.
igbo: Ahụ ihu ofe, asụta ụtara

meaning: An unexpected, elusive, or highly unusual action leaves opponents or onlookers completely baffled and unable to react.
literal: Farting while up in the air confuses the flies.
usage: This is used to describe a clever, unpredictable move that completely disorients one's rivals or critics.
igbo: Ahụrụ anyụrụ n'elu gbara ijiji gharị

meaning: Overstaying one's welcome or being too familiar leads to a loss of respect and hospitality.
literal: When an in-law is seen too often, they are no longer offered a seat.
usage: This is used to warn someone against visiting too frequently or overstaying their welcome to preserve their dignity.
equivalent: Familiarity breeds contempt
igbo: Ahụshie ọgọ a nazịghị asị ya were oche

meaning: Difficult circumstances force people to adopt a hostile or suspicious outlook on life.
literal: A bad situation brings about looking with a bad eye.
usage: Used to explain or excuse someone's defensive or bitter attitude due to their harsh circumstances.
igbo: Ajọ ọnọdụ butere ile ajọ anya

meaning: A wicked or troublesome child brings unnatural sorrow and shame to their parents.
literal: A bad child entered his mother's womb through the backyard.
usage: Used to lament the birth or behavior of a highly problematic child who causes endless grief.
igbo: Ajọ nwa siri owere baa nne ya afọ

meaning: Hard work leads to prosperity and comfort.
literal: Dusty hands bring about an oily mouth.
usage: Used to encourage someone to work hard or to justify the reward of a diligent worker.
equivalent: No pain, no gain
igbo: Aka aja aja na-ebute ọnụ mmanụ mmanụ

meaning: Truth or greatness cannot be hidden or suppressed by human effort.
literal: The hand cannot cover the moon.
usage: Used to assert that a person's obvious talent or the undeniable truth of a matter cannot be concealed.
equivalent: Truth will out
igbo: Aka ekpuchi ọnwa

meaning: When the strongest or most powerful among us falls, the weak realize they stand no chance.
literal: If the hand breaks iron, fear grips the wood.
usage: Used as a warning or observation when a formidable person or institution is defeated, signaling danger to lesser ones.
igbo: Aka gbajie igwe ụjọ atụọ osisi

meaning: [uncertain] A person's actions or external influences are responsible for another's defensive or hardened state.
literal: The hand that makes the fish grow scales.
usage: Used to point out that someone's difficult behavior was caused by how they were treated.
igbo: Aka na-eme azụ gbaa nkụrụkụ

meaning: Mutual cooperation and assistance are necessary for mutual benefit and cleanliness.
literal: If the right hand washes the left hand, the left hand washes the right hand.
usage: Used to encourage cooperation, mutual aid, or reciprocity in a community or relationship.
equivalent: One hand washes the other
igbo: Aka nri kwọọ aka ekpe, aka ekpe a kwọọ aka nri

meaning: Proper discipline and correction do not harm a child but rather build their character.
literal: The hand of training does not kill a child.
usage: Used to justify disciplining a child or to reassure a parent that firm upbringing is beneficial.
equivalent: Spare the rod and spoil the child
igbo: Aka ọmụmụ anaghị egbu nwa

meaning: Securing resources or food is as good as consuming them, as the hardest part of the task is done.
literal: Once the hand reaches the bag, it has reached the mouth.
usage: Used to express confidence that a goal is virtually achieved once the primary obstacle is overcome.
igbo: Aka ruru akpa, eru go ọnụ

meaning: Little contributions or consistent small efforts eventually lead to abundance.
literal: Hand brings, hand brings, it fills the mouth.
usage: Used to encourage steady, small savings or collaborative contributions toward a larger goal.
equivalent: Many a mickle makes a muckle
igbo: Aka wete aka wete, o ju ọnụ

meaning: Certain things, like love, gossip, or natural disasters, cannot be restricted by artificial boundaries.
literal: The climbing bean does not know the boundary of the land.
usage: Used to explain why an issue or relationship has spread beyond its expected limits.
igbo: Akịdị anaghị ama oke ala

meaning: Discretion and common sense are essential for survival and well-being.
literal: Wisdom is life.
usage: Used to advise someone to act with caution, tact, and wisdom rather than brute force.
equivalent: Discretion is the better part of valor
igbo: Ako bụ ndụ

meaning: Proper planning and mutual agreement prevent future conflicts and ensure peace of mind.
literal: When things are discussed, one sleeps comfortably on the mat.
usage: Used to advocate for open discussion and consensus before embarking on a joint venture.
igbo: Akpaa akpa, arụhụo n'ute

meaning: Hard work during one's youth or productive years ensures a comfortable and restful retirement.
literal: If one gathers in the sun, one eats in the shade.
usage: Used to motivate someone to endure present hardships for future comfort.
igbo: Akpaa n'anwụ e rie na ndụ

meaning: Wealth is transient and constantly changes hands, never staying with one person forever.
literal: Wealth is like water in a mortar; it flows this way and flows that way.
usage: Used to counsel humility to the rich or to comfort the poor by reminding them of the shifting nature of fortune.
equivalent: Riches have wings
igbo: Akụ dịka mmiri nọ n'ikwe, o ruga ebe a, o ruga ebe a

meaning: No matter how high or far someone roams, they will eventually settle down or fall to their ultimate destiny.
literal: After the flying termite flies around, it falls for the young toad.
usage: Used to note that pride, restlessness, or high-flying status will eventually come to a humble end.
igbo: Akụ ferechaa ọ daara nwa awọ

meaning: True success is measured by the tangible benefits one brings back to their home or community.
literal: When wealth reaches home, the one who gathered it becomes known.
usage: Used to encourage diaspora members to invest in their homelands or to praise someone who has brought honor home.
igbo: Akụ rue ụlọ a mara onye kpara ya

meaning: [uncertain] This narrative or excuse is completely useless and yields no practical results.
literal: This story is like a hole that does not roast cocoyam.
usage: Used to dismiss an unproductive discussion, a tall tale, or an ineffective excuse.
igbo: Akụkọ a bụ oghere ji egheghi ede

meaning: [uncertain] Novelty often comes with unexpected flaws or initial difficulties.
literal: A new cloth leaks urine.
usage: Used to caution someone not to be overly excited by new acquisitions or situations that have not been tested.
igbo: Akwa ọhụrụ na-apụ maamiri

meaning: When an underdog achieves a feat that the strong failed to do, it brings great embarrassment to the strong.
literal: If a chicken's egg cracks a palm nut, the stone will be ashamed.
usage: Used to mock a powerful person who failed at a task that a weak or minor person easily accomplished.
igbo: Akwa ọkụkọ tie akị, ihere emee nkume

meaning: Two flawed or corrupt things deserve each other, or a bad situation perfectly matches another bad situation.
literal: A rotten palm nut and a dented mortar.
usage: Used to describe a perfect match between two bad or useless things.
igbo: Akwụ rere ere na ikwe mpu

meaning: Societal instability or chaos benefits those in power who exploit the situation for their own gain.
literal: A land that is not good is the gain of the titled elders.
usage: A lamentation or rebuke when leaders exploit a crisis instead of resolving it.
igbo: Ala adịghị mma bụ uru ndi nze

meaning: Treating a sacred, noble, or innocent thing with the same disrespect or cheapness as a common or dirty thing.
literal: Knowing the firewood that was used to roast a rat, and saying it should be used to roast a dove.
usage: A warning or rebuke against desecrating something valuable or treating an innocent person like a criminal.
igbo: Amara nkụ ahụ e jiri hụọ oke, sị were ya hụọ kpalakuku

meaning: If you live long enough and remain patient, you will eventually enjoy the pleasures and rewards of life.
literal: A penis that does not die prematurely will eat hairy meat.
usage: An encouragement to be patient and stay alive to witness better days.
equivalent: All things come to those who wait
igbo: Amụ na-anwụchụghị anwụchi ga-eri anụ gbara aji

meaning: Avoiding unnecessary reliance on unreliable or easily distracted people to prevent disappointment.
literal: I do not ask a child to lift a chair for me; if his mother does not call him, his father will call him.
usage: Used to assert one's independence or to decline help from someone who is likely to be called away or distracted.
igbo: Anaghị m asị nwata buliere m n'oche, nne ya akpọghị ya nna ya akpọọ ya

meaning: Extraordinary or extreme situations require equally extraordinary or extreme measures.
literal: If an animal runs an extraordinary run, it is shot with an extraordinary gun.
usage: Used to justify taking drastic measures to solve a particularly difficult or stubborn problem.
equivalent: Desperate diseases require desperate remedies
igbo: Anụ gbaa ajọ ọsọ, a gbaa ya ajọ egbe

meaning: When multiple troubles occur, one wonders why the most innocent or vulnerable is the one suffering the worst blow.
literal: Let the bee sting, let the wasp sting, but what has blinded my little puppy?
usage: A lamentation when an innocent bystander or vulnerable person bears the brunt of a conflict.
igbo: Aṅụ gọọ, ebu gọọ, gịnị gbakpọkwaranụ nwa nkịta m anya

meaning: A temporary setback is not the end of the world; there will always be another opportunity.
literal: If the animal escapes today, tomorrow is another day of hunting.
usage: Used as a consolation or encouragement after a failure or missed opportunity.
equivalent: Tomorrow is another day
igbo: Anụ laa taa echi bụ nta

meaning: Those who act early or arrive first get the best opportunities.
literal: The animal that arrives first drinks clean water.
usage: Used to encourage promptness, early action, or punctuality.
equivalent: The early bird catches the worm
igbo: Anụ mbu ụzọ na-aṅụ mmiri ọma

meaning: Trying to imitate someone with unique abilities or resources beyond your own will only lead to self-harm.
literal: An animal that tries to follow the monkey will break its leg.
usage: A warning against foolish imitation or trying to compete with those far above one's station.
igbo: Anụ soro enwe o majie ụkwụ

meaning: Once a formidable threat is overcome or dead, it is easy to underestimate how dangerous it once was.
literal: When a leopard's skin is bought, it seems as if the leopard was a harmless animal.
usage: A cautionary reminder not to trivialize a past danger or the struggles of those who overcame it.
igbo: Anụta akara eze, ọ dịka eze ọ gwọrọ anụmanụ

meaning: Anyone who defeats a notoriously tough opponent must be exceptionally formidable themselves.
literal: The beast that bites a dog to death must have a terrible bite.
usage: Used to acknowledge the superior strength or capability of someone who has overcome a major challenge or rival.
igbo: Anụ tagburu nkịta na-ata ajọ arụ

meaning: Do not settle for a lesser or temporary pleasure when a much better and more lasting reward is on the way.
literal: Do not drink raffia palm wine when the oil palm wine is coming.
usage: An admonition to exercise patience and hold out for a superior opportunity rather than settling prematurely.
igbo: Aṅụla ngwọ na nkwụ na-abịa

meaning: Some truths or qualities are so obvious that they do not require testing or elaborate proof.
literal: It is with the eyes that one knows a ripe corn.
usage: Used to assert that a situation or person's character is clear and obvious to anyone who looks.
igbo: Anya ka e ji ama ọka chara acha

meaning: I cherish your presence and hope we remain together in good health for a long time.
literal: May the eye with which I see you not go blind.
usage: A warm expression of appreciation, affection, or goodwill upon seeing a beloved friend or relative.
igbo: Anya m hụrụ gị akpọla m

meaning: One should appreciate and celebrate rare, beautiful, or exceptional opportunities when they arise.
literal: The eye that sees an eagle should praise it, because the eagle is not seen every day.
usage: Used to encourage people to show gratitude or admiration for rare blessings or extraordinary achievements.
igbo: Anya hụrụ ugo jaa ya mma maka na a naghị ahụ ugo kwa daa

meaning: A confrontation or test will eventually reveal who is truly strong, capable, or in the right.
literal: We shall know which of the two tortoises is the male.
usage: A challenge issued before a contest or dispute to indicate that the truth or victor will soon be made clear.
igbo: Anyị ga-ama mbe naabụ nke bụ oke

meaning: It is absurd when the offender acts like the victim or complains louder than the person they harmed.
literal: The millipede that was stepped on did not cry, yet the person who stepped on it is crying.
usage: A rebuke against someone who causes harm but then plays the victim or complains about the situation.
igbo: Ariri azọrọ ụkwụ ebeghi akwa, ọ bụrụ onye zọrọ ya ụkwụ na-ebe akwa

meaning: If an evil or corrupt practice is tolerated for too long, it becomes accepted as normal behavior.
literal: When an abomination lasts for a year, it becomes a tradition.
usage: A warning against tolerating bad behavior or corruption, urging immediate corrective action before it becomes entrenched.
igbo: Arụ gbaa afọ, o buru omenaala

meaning: If a subordinate or someone you helped create becomes too arrogant, they must be reminded of their humble origins.
literal: If a deity becomes too troublesome, it is shown the wood from which it was carved.
usage: A stern warning or rebuke to put an arrogant or rebellious subordinate back in their place.
igbo: Arụsị kpakarịa ike, e gosi ya osisi e jiri pịa ya

meaning: Destroying local protectors or valuable allies during internal squabbles leaves a community vulnerable to external threats.
literal: If a hero is killed in a home war, when an outside war comes people start looking for the hero.
usage: Used as a warning against harming one's own key defenders during internal disputes.
igbo: E gbuo dike n'ọgụ ụlọ, e rue n'ọgụ ama achọwa dike

meaning: Even when taking drastic action in anger, one must retain enough composure and sense to act properly in the end.
literal: If killed in anger, one buries with the head intact.
usage: Used to urge self-restraint and moderation even during moments of intense anger or conflict.
igbo: E gbuo ma iwe, e lie ma isi

meaning: Opening a path or opportunity allows free expression and open discussion to take place.
literal: If the door is opened, the mouth is opened.
usage: Reached for to encourage open dialogue once a meeting or discussion has officially been initiated.
igbo: E gupee ụzọ, e gupee ọnụ

meaning: You do not need a complex test to recognize obvious quality or maturity; it is evident at a glance.
literal: One uses the eye to know mature corn.
usage: Used to point out that someone's expertise, maturity, or quality is obvious to any observer.
igbo: E ji anya ama ọka kara aka

meaning: Small initial signs reveal the true, unpleasant nature of what is to follow.
literal: One uses the smell of a fart to gauge the foulness of feces.
usage: Used as a warning that minor unpleasant signs indicate a much bigger problem ahead.
igbo: E ji isi ahụrụ ama ụtọ nsi

meaning: It takes money to make money.
literal: One uses a seed token to win another seed token.
usage: Reached for to justify spending resources or making an initial investment in order to secure greater profit.
equivalent: It takes money to make money.
igbo: E ji okwe eri okwe

meaning: If you fail to disarm or subdue an opponent while you have the upper hand, you will lose the chance once they recover.
literal: If a warrior is pinned to the ground and his knife is not seized, is it when he stands up?
usage: Used to advise taking decisive action to eliminate a threat or secure a victory while the opportunity exists.
igbo: E jide dike n'ala ma e kwotaghị ya mma, ọ bụzi mgbe o biliri ọtọ

meaning: Having a secure fallback makes it easy to speak lightly about hardship or famine.
literal: Holding a piece of yam in hand, one tells the story of famine.
usage: Used as a rebuke against people who preach about suffering from a position of security and comfort.
igbo: E jide ibe ji n’aka e were kọwa akụkọ maka ụganị

meaning: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
literal: The hawk has not even been caught, yet people say a woman will not eat it.
usage: Used to reprimand people who are prematurely disputing the sharing of unacquired gains.
equivalent: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
igbo: E jidebeghi egbe, a na-ekwu na nwaanyị agaghị eri ya

meaning: Wasted effort performed in secret or in the dark achieves nothing because no one can see it.
literal: One does not wink at the night.
usage: Used to admonish someone performing a futile action in secret where it will have no effect.
igbo: E jighi abalị arọ anya

meaning: Wealth is accumulated through saving and prudent management, not merely by earning and squandering.
literal: One does not become rich by earning and squandering.
usage: Used as a rebuke against wasteful spending and to encourage prudent financial management.
igbo: E jighi akpata atụfuo aba ọgaranya

meaning: People turn to prayer or seek divine intervention primarily when they are facing distress or trouble.
literal: One does not enter a house of prayer with good eyes.
usage: Used to explain why someone is seeking help or attending prayer, highlighting that hardship drives people to seek aid.
igbo: E jighi anya ọma aba ụka ekpere

meaning: God provides the necessary means and strength to handle whatever burden or task He bestows upon a person.
literal: The God who gave a poor person a yam will also give him a digging stick to harvest it.
usage: Spoken to encourage someone facing a daunting task, reassuring them that they will receive the resources needed to succeed.
igbo: Chi nyere nwa ogbenye ji ga-enye ya mbazụ ọ ga-eji egwuru ya

meaning: This too shall pass.
literal: Bedbug told her children that whatever is hot will eventually become cold.
usage: Spoken to console someone enduring a painful situation, advising them to stay patient until relief arrives.
equivalent: This too shall pass.
igbo: Chinchi sị ụmụ ya ihe dị ọkụ ga jụ oyi

meaning: When looking for a solution or a lost item, one must return to the place or origin where the trouble first started.
literal: Look for your clothes where you took your bath.
usage: Spoken as advice to someone attempting to solve a crisis by searching in the wrong place or ignoring the root cause.
igbo: Chọwa akwa gi ebe ị sara ahụ

meaning: Physician, heal thyself.
literal: Does the native doctor who cures diarrhea keep his own buttocks on the rafters?
usage: Spoken as a rebuke against an expert or critic who fails to address their own obvious personal flaws or troubles.
equivalent: Physician, heal thyself.
igbo: Dibịa na-agwọ otoro, o dewere ike ya n'uko?

meaning: A person's true strength and competence become visible when they are tested by a tough challenge.
literal: When a strong man chews a palm kernel, one sees his jaw muscles working.
usage: Spoken in praise of a capable person who demonstrates resilience and capability in times of hardship.
igbo: Dike taa akị, ahụ ikikere ya

meaning: Receiving help from a subordinate or inferior does not mean one should abandon proper boundaries and bow down to them.
literal: A hunter will not, because a big dog caught game for him, call it his mother's husband.
usage: Spoken to remind someone to maintain proper dignity and boundaries even after receiving assistance from a subordinate.
igbo: Dinta agaghị asi maka oke nkịta jideere ya anụ kpọọ ya di nne ya

meaning: Discretion in speech is essential, as a wise person does not blab everything they observe or know.
literal: A palm wine tapper does not say everything he sees from the top of the palm tree.
usage: Spoken to caution someone against revealing secrets or oversharing sensitive information.
igbo: Diochi anaghị ekwucha ihe niile ọ hụrụ n'elu nkwụ

meaning: Formal courtesies and escorting guests are tokens of goodwill rather than essential requirements for a traveler to reach home.
literal: "Escort me out" is mere affection, for no one sets off for home without eventually arriving.
usage: Spoken to acknowledge warm hospitality or politely dismiss unnecessary fuss over a departing guest.
igbo: Dupu m bụ ure, o nweghi onye lawara nụ ma ghara ilarụ

meaning: People rarely feel the true weight or grief of another person's tragedy until it touches them personally.
literal: When another person's corpse is carried, it feels like carrying a bundle of firewood.
usage: Spoken to rebuke indifference and point out how detached outsiders can be toward someone else's suffering.
igbo: E buru ozu onye ọzọ, ọ dịka ebu ukwu nkụ

meaning: If one listens carefully and pays close attention, subtle truths and hidden matters will be revealed.
literal: If one places an ear to the ground, one hears the footfalls of ants.
usage: Spoken to urge someone to pay close attention and stay vigilant to detect subtle warning signs.
igbo: E che nti n’ala, a nụ ụda ụkwụ agbụsi

meaning: A coward displays bravado and acts tough only after the danger has been defused by others.
literal: When a fight is settled, the coward begins to boast.
usage: Spoken to mock or rebuke someone who acts brave only after a conflict has already ended safely.
igbo: E gboo ọgụ, onye ụjọ a na-aba

meaning: A leopard cannot change its spots.
literal: Even if a hawk is slaughtered a bull, its eyes will still be on a little chick.
usage: Spoken to criticize someone who continues to engage in petty or bad habits despite receiving great good fortune or elevated status.
equivalent: A leopard cannot change its spots.
igbo: E gbugodiri egbe ehi, anya ya ka ga-adịkwa na nwa shiishii

meaning: Civility and friendliness open doors and make people pleasant to deal with.
literal: When greetings are answered, the face becomes bright.
usage: Used to encourage politeness and acknowledge how warmly a friendly gesture is received.
igbo: E kwe ekele, ihu asaa

meaning: If you are overly accommodating to someone notorious for taking advantage, they will push their demands even further.
literal: If you shake hands with a leper, he desires to embrace you.
usage: Used as a warning against letting toxic or greedy people cross your boundaries.
igbo: E kwe onye ekpenta n'aka, ibi ọma agụwa ya

meaning: Never underestimate seemingly small or insignificant things, because they can cause major damage.
